paragraphs: For about one month, from March 18 to April 16, 2023, I was allowed to do a clinical study abroad at Korea University in Seoul, South Korea. For the first two weeks I did the clerkship in emergency medicine, and for the next two weeks in neurology. In South Korea, a country enormously popular around the world today, I received a great deal of help and gained very valuable experiences. Below I describe what I learned from this study abroad.

First, I will describe life in Seoul. Prices are low, public safety is as good as in Japan, and I could go out alone without worry. I stayed at a hotel in a neighborhood called "Jongno 3-ga," about 15 minutes by subway from the university. Living alone itself was a new challenge, but apart from laundry the hotel staff took care of everything, so I was very comfortable. Access to the university was also very good, and I had no trouble commuting. In addition, it was near popular spots in Korea such as Myeongdong and Itaewon, and I think it was an ideal place for enjoying sightseeing as well. And just as there are many people in Japan who like Korea, there were also many people in Korea who like Japan. Most of the people I spoke with had been to Japan and talked happily about their memories of Japan. Incidentally, Fukuoka and Okinawa were particularly popular. I was also often greeted in Japanese with "ohayou gozaimasu" or "arigatou gozaimasu," which made me somehow happy. I myself could hardly speak Korean, but I made full use of the Google Translate app, so I had no trouble communicating at all. Still, I think it would have been good to learn Korean in order to enjoy Korean culture more. Perhaps because of the national character, Korean people are generous, and I was impressed that when I asked for directions, they explained very kindly. At the restaurant I frequented, the staff spoke to me cheerfully and gave me a refill of kimchi every time, which is also a good memory.

Next, I will describe the clerkship. I did my clerkship at Korea University Anam Hospital. In each department, doctors were assigned to me and supported me kindly. Rounds and conferences were all held in Korean, so there were parts I could not understand, but the doctors later explained them to me in English in an easy-to-understand way, which was reassuring. Also, a big difference from Japanese hospitals was that disease names and symptoms were expressed in English. English was used for these both in charts and orally, and I got the impression that English is more familiar in medicine than in Japan. In emergency medicine, I was able to observe the doctors' work flow up close. Since I will start working as a junior resident next year and thought it important to have an image of emergency work, it was a very good experience. Conferences began at 8:00 every morning, with case reports and journal clubs, and I was stimulated by the doctors' eager attitude. In the field, I learned in particular about the importance of triage. Triage means prioritizing the treatment of the sick and injured according to urgency and severity in order to provide effective care with limited resources. Korea University Anam Hospital is a hospital proud of being among the largest in Korea, and a great many patients are brought to the emergency department every day. I was taught that in such a large hospital in particular, maintaining the quality of emergency care by setting priorities is indispensable. This applies to emergency care in Japan too, and I was able to reaffirm that I will need to do triage myself. In neurology, I was able to deepen my understanding mainly of diseases such as cerebral infarction and moyamoya disease. Honestly, I could not find many points that differ from Japanese neurology, but I think it was good to learn neurological diseases from an angle different from usual. I was taught that cerebral infarction is a common disease regardless of country, that rapid treatment and response are needed in the acute phase, and that even when the condition stabilizes a little, symptoms can fluctuate, so continuous monitoring is necessary. For moyamoya disease, I was allowed to examine an actual ward patient and gave a case report. This disease is common in Asia, particularly Japan, Korea and China, and it was a topic closely related to us. In addition, the doctors asked me the meaning of the Japanese word "moyamoya." When I explained in English, "It means being muddled or having a lingering knot in one's heart," they understood, which is a good memory for me personally. I also gave presentations in both departments on the differences in doctors' careers between Japan and Korea. This was not only requested by the doctors, but also a field I had been interested in myself for some time, and it was a good opportunity to output. Attending medical school for six years and taking a little over ten years from university entrance to obtaining specialist qualification are the same in both, but I found that there are two major differences between them. The first is the career immediately after graduating from university. In Japan one works for two years as initial residency, whereas in Korea one moves on to a one-year period called "internship." The significance is almost the same, and in both it is important to rotate through various departments and decide which specialty to enter, but I was surprised that the period is half as long in Korea. The second is that Korea has a system of working as a "public health doctor (PHD)."

PHD refers to male doctors in Korea who, instead of military service, work for three years in areas without doctors, in airport quarantine and so on. The period of serving as a PHD can be chosen according to each person's career path, but they are reportedly mostly in their twenties and thirties. During the COVID-19 pandemic, PHDs played a major role on the front line of Korean healthcare, collecting PCR test specimens. In addition, at the end of the clerkship I was treated to samgyeopsal. Everything from dividing the soup and salad to cutting the meat was left to the doctors, and here too I could feel the doctors' spirit of hospitality. Not only was the authentic samgyeopsal of course the most delicious, but the chamisul I drank with the meal was also exceptional. At the hospital and the university campus there were students from various countries besides Korea, such as Mongolia and Germany, and I had many opportunities to talk. I could feel differences in values from Japanese people, and my horizons broadened. Many students also liked Japanese anime culture, and I was glad to be able to get excited talking about works such as "ONE PIECE" and "Studio Ghibli."

Until this study abroad, I had never lived alone or traveled abroad alone, and before departure I was anxious about whether I could live properly. However, I was treated kindly by the university doctors, the office staff, students, and the local people outside the university, and I was able to have a fruitful study abroad in a comfortable environment. I strongly felt that from now on, when I meet people who have come from overseas in Japan, I want to become a person who thinks about what I can do for them and contributes. I am also sincerely grateful to my parents, who supported me financially. And finally, I would like to express my gratitude to Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and the doctors of the International Collaboration Office who supported me throughout the whole process related to study abroad, and to the people of Korea University. Thank you very much.
